<h>Lectio 1</h>
Léctio sancti Evangélii secúndum Ioánnem
<r>Ioannes 8:12-20</r>
<c>I</c>n illo témpore: Locútus est Iesus turbis Iudæórum, dicens: Ego sum lux mundi: qui séquitur me, non ámbulat in ténebris, sed habébit lumen vitæ. Et réliqua.

Homilía sancti Augustíni Epíscopi
<r>Tract. 34 in Ioannem, post init.</r>
<c>Q</c>uod ait Dóminus: Ego sum lux mundi: clarum puto esse eis, qui habent óculos, unde huius lucis partícipes fiant: qui autem non habent óculos, nisi in sola carne, mirántur quod dictum est a Dómino Iesu Christo: Ego sum lux mundi. Et forte non desit qui dicat apud semetípsum: Numquid forte Dóminus Christus est sol iste, qui ortu et occásu péragit diem? Non enim defuérunt hærétici, qui ista sensérunt.

<h>Reading 1</h>
Continuation of the Holy Gospel according to John
<r>John 8:12-20</r>
<c>A</c>t that time, Jesus spoke to the multitude of Jews saying: I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life. And so on.

Homily on this passage by St. Augustine, Bishop <n>of Hippo.</n>
<r>34th Tract on John</r>
<c>I</c> take it that these words of the Lord: “I am the Light of the world” are sufficiently clear to all men who have eyes which see that Light. At the same time, such men as have no eyes except those which are in their bodies, are surprised to find our Lord Jesus Christ saying, “I am the Light of the world”. And that we might not want somebody to say, “Is our Lord Jesus Christ, then, the same sun that riseth and setteth every day?” There have actually been heretics who did say it. The Manicheans believed that that sun which we see with our bodily eyes, and to see which is plain and common to beasts as well as men, was the Lord Christ.
<r>℣.</r> But thou, O Lord, have mercy upon us.
<r>℟.</r> Thanks be to God.

<h>Reading 2</h>
Continuation of the Holy Gospel according to John
<r>John 8:12-20</r>
<c>A</c>t that time, Jesus spoke to the multitude of Jews saying: I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life. And so on.

Homily on this passage by St. Augustine, Bishop <n>of Hippo.</n>
<r>34th Tract on John</r>
<c>I</c> take it that these words of the Lord: “I am the Light of the world” are sufficiently clear to all men who have eyes which see that Light. At the same time, such men as have no eyes except those which are in their bodies, are surprised to find our Lord Jesus Christ saying, “I am the Light of the world”. And that we might not want somebody to say, “Is our Lord Jesus Christ, then, the same sun that riseth and setteth every day?” There have actually been heretics who did say it. The Manicheans believed that that sun which we see with our bodily eyes, and to see which is plain and common to beasts as well as men, was the Lord Christ. But the right faith of the Catholic Church damneth such comment, and recogniseth in it a doctrine of devils. And as it is her practice not only to brand errors by the difference of her own Creed, but also to remove them, if possible, by dint of argument, let us take up arms against this falsehood, which hath from the very beginning been the object of the curse of the Holy Church. God forbid that we should believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is this sun whose apparent movement is to rise every day in the East, and set every day in the West; which when we see no more, night cometh over us; and whose rays are sometimes intercepted by clouds and which hath some law of motion of its own whereby it describeth an orbit. The planet is not the same thing as our Lord Jesus Christ. Our Lord Jesus Christ is not that created sun, but He by Whom that sun was created; for all things were made by Him, and without Him was not anything made that was made. <n>John i. 30</n>
<r>℣.</r> But thou, O Lord, have mercy upon us.
<r>℟.</r> Thanks be to God.

<r>℟.</r> Ecce mitto Angelum meum, qui præcédat te, et custódiat semper: obsérva et audi vocem meam, et inimícus ero inimícis tuis, et affligéntes te afflígam:
* Et præcédet te Angelus meus.

<h>Lectio 3</h>
<c>N</c>on est Dóminus Christus sol factus, sed per quem sol factus est. Est ergo lux, quæ fecit hanc lucem. Hanc amémus, hanc intellégere cupiámus, ipsam sitíamus, ut ad ipsam duce ipsa aliquándo veniámus: et in illa ita vivámus, ut nunquam omníno moriámur. Ista enim lux est, de qua prophetía olim præmíssa ita in Psalmo cécinit: Quóniam apud te est fons vitæ, et in lúmine tuo vidébimus lumen.
<r>℣.</r> Tu autem, Dómine, miserére nostri.
<r>℟.</r> Deo grátias.

<h>Reading 3</h>
<c>N</c>on est Dóminus Christus sol factus, sed per quem sol factus est. He is therefore the Light by Whom the material light was made. Him may we love, Him may we long to know, Him may we thirst after; to Him may His own beams one day lead us, and in Him may we so live that we shall never die! For He, even He, and none other, He is that Light, of Whom the Prophet that was given of old time sang in the Psalms, when he said: “For with thee is the fountain of life, and in thy Light shall we see light.” <n>Ps. xxxv. 10.</n> Remember ye likewise what the word of God's ancient saints saith of such Light: “O Lord, Thou preservest man and beast! How excellent is thy loving-kindness, O God!” <n>7, 8.</n>

<h>Martyrologium</h>
<c>P</c>rídie Idus Mártii Luna sexta. Anno Dómini 2027
<h>D</h>omínica Passiónis.
<h>R</h>omæ, in agro Veráno, sancti Leónis, Epíscopi et Mártyris.
<h>I</h>tem Romæ natális sanctórum quadragínta septem Mártyrum, qui baptizáti sunt a beáto Apóstolo Petro, cum tenerétur in custódia Mamertíni cum Coapóstolo suo Paulo, ubi novem menses deténti sunt; qui omnes, sub devotíssima fídei confessióne, Neroniáno gládio consúmpti sunt.
<h>I</h>n Província Valériæ sanctórum duórum Monachórum, quos Longobárdi suspéndio necavérunt in árbore; in qua Mártyres, licet defúncti, ab hóstibus ipsis audíti sunt psállere.
<h>I</h>n ea étiam persecutióne Diáconus Ecclésiæ Marsicánæ, in confessióne fídei, cápite truncátus est.
<h>I</h>n Africa sanctórum Mártyrum Petri et Aphrodísii, qui, in persecutióne Wandálica, martýrii corónam percepérunt.
<h>C</h>arrhis, in Mesopotámia, sancti Eutýchii patrícii, et Sociórum, qui ab Evelid, Arabum Rege, ob fídei confessiónem, interémpti sunt.
<h>H</h>alberstátti, in Germánia, dormítio beátæ Mathíldis Regínæ, matris Othónis Primi, Romanórum Imperatóris, humilitáte et patiéntia conspícuæ.
<r>℣.</r> Et álibi aliórum plurimórum sanctórum Mártyrum et Confessórum, atque sanctárum Vírginum.
<r>℟.</r> Deo grátias.
b.e1664e35c6:
<h>Martyrology</h>
<c>M</c>arch 14th 2027, the 6th day of the Moon, were born into the better life:
<h>T</h>he Sunday of the Passion.
<h>A</h>t Rome, in the Veranian field, the holy martyr Leo, Bishop.
<h>L</h>ikewise at Rome, forty-seven holy martyrs, who were all baptized by the blessed Apostle Peter during the nine months during which he and his fellow-Apostle Paul were imprisoned in the Mamertine prison, and who, all for the loyal confession of their faith, were slain by the sword, under the Emperor Nero.
<h>I</h>n the province of Valeria, two holy monks, whom the Lombards hung upon a tree, whereon after they were dead their very enemies heard them singing.
<h>I</h>n the same persecution, a Deacon of the church of Maruvium, [now called that of Pescina,] was beheaded for confessing the faith.
<h>I</h>n Africa, the holy martyrs Peter and Aphrodisius, who received their crown in the persecution under the Vandals.
<h>A</h>t Haran, in Mesopotamia, the holy martyrs Eutychius the Patrician and his Companions, who were slain by Evelid, King of the Arabs, for confessing their faith, [in the year 741.]
<h>A</h>t Halberstadt, in Germany, the blessed Matilda, Queen of the Romans, Mother of the Emperor Otto I, who fell asleep in peace, illustrious for her lowliness and long suffering, [in the year 968.]
<r>℣.</r> And elsewhere many other holy martyrs, confessors, and holy virgins.
<r>℟.</r> Thanks be to God.

<r>Hymn</r>
<c>A</c>broad the regal banners fly,
Now shines the cross’s mystery;
Upon it Life did death endure,
And yet by death did life procure.

<h>W</h>ho, wounded with a direful spear,
Did, purposely to wash us clear
From stain of sin, pour out a flood
Of precious water mixed with blood.

<h>T</h>hat which the prophet-king of old
Hath in mysterious verse foretold,
Is now accomplished, whilst we see
God ruling nations from a tree.

<h>O</h> lovely and refulgent tree,
Adorned with purpled majesty;
Culled from a worthy stock, to bear
Those limbs which sanctifièd were.

<h>B</h>lest tree, whose happy branches bore
The wealth that did the world restore;
The beam that did that body weigh
Which raised up hell’s expected prey.

<r>The following verse is said on bended knee.</r>

<h>O</h> Cross, our one reliance, hail!
This holy Passiontide avail
To give fresh merit to the saint,
And pardon to the penitent.

<h>B</h>lest Trinity, salvation’s spring,
May every soul thy praises sing;
To those thou grantest conquest by
The holy cross, rewards apply.
Amen.
